blocks.text: It is proved that תנשמת thinsemeth is the little owl.

The word תנשמת thinsemeth is highly ambiguous among the Hebrews. For in Levit. XI, 30. it is [col. 286] among the species of lizards, as was said in its place. But in the eighteenth verse of the same chapter, with which we are dealing, it is a kind of unclean bird. The Greeks explain it as πορφυρίωνα [porphyriōna], a water bird in Libya and Commagene in Syria, so called from the colour of its beak and feet, for its feathers are blue ^{(1)}. Jerome here has swan. Jonathan has אותיא otja, that is, otus, as I at least think: a bird very different in nature from the bustard (otis), although close to it in name. For the otus is a nocturnal bird, about which the Philosopher writes thus in book 8, chapter 12: Ὁ δὲ ὠτὸς, ὅμοιος ταῖς γλαυξὶ, καὶ περὶ τὰ ὦτα πτερύγια ἔχων. ἔνιοι δὲ αὐτὸν νυκτικόρακα καλοῦσιν. ἔστι δὲ κόβαλος, καὶ μιμητὴς, καὶ ἀντορχούμενος ἁλίσκεται, περιελθόντος θατέρου τῶν θηρευτῶν, καθάπερ γλαύξ. [Ho de ōtos, homoios tais glauxi, kai peri ta ōta pterygia echōn. enioi de auton nyktikoraka kalousin. esti de kobalos, kai mimētēs, kai antorchoumenos halisketai, perielthontos thaterou tōn thēreutōn, kathaper glaux.] “The otus is similar to little owls, and has little feathers around its ears” (hence its name). “Some call it the night raven. It is a buffoon and a mimic. And while it dances in turn opposite one of the fowlers who is dancing, it is caught by the other, who goes round it, like the little owl” ^{(2)}. Onkelos has בותא bautha, or bavetha, also a kind of nocturnal bird, which in Greek is called βύας [byas], in Latin bubo [eagle owl], and in Arabic البوه [al-būh] albuho, from its cry. Yet even among the Arabs it is hardly agreed what البوه [al-būh] albuho properly is. Damir: البوه طاير يشبه البوم الا انه اصغر منه والانثي بوهة ويشبه بها الرجل الاحمق [al-būh ṭāyir yushbih al-būm illā annahu aṣghar minhu wa-l-unthī būha wa-yushabbah bihā al-rajul al-aḥmaq]: “Albuho is a bird similar to album, that is, to the eagle owl, except that it is smaller. The feminine is albuha. A man who is stupid is compared to it.” After proving this by an example taken from a certain poet, he adds: وقيل البوه ذكر البوم وقيل البوه اكبر من البوم [wa-qīla al-būh dhakar al-būm wa-qīla al-būh akbar min al-būm]: “By some albuho is said to be the male of album, and again by others to be larger than album,” that is, the eagle owl. Which is most true. For البوه [al-būh] albuho is certainly the Greek βύας [byas], that is, bubo, the largest of the nocturnal birds. Nor is the Chaldee בותא anything else; it is formed, after the manner of the language, from בוא, as עותא, iniquity, from עוא, and כותא, window, from כוא.
